<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults are particularly vulnerable to nutritional deficiencies and age-related loss of muscle mass and function, which may converge as malnutrition, functional decline, frailty, and mortality. Despite growing recognition of its clinical significance, the prevalence of malnutrition in this population across care settings remains unclear. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of malnutrition among older adults with sarcopenia and to examine factors moderating its prevalence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted using six databases (CINAHL, Cochrane Library, Embase, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science) from inception to March 2025. Studies reporting malnutrition prevalence in older adults with sarcopenia were included. Pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects model with the Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation. Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran’s Q test and the I² statistic, and moderator analyses were performed to explore sources of heterogeneity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Forty-one studies involving 9,122 older adults (mean age 72.7 ± 6.3 years) were included. The pooled prevalence of malnutrition was 26.6% (95% CI: 20.3–34.2). Prevalence was highest in hospital settings (34.6%; 95% CI: 26.1–44.1), followed by institutional (23.0%; 95% CI: 11.8–40.1) and community settings (18.7%; 95% CI: 9.1–34.5). Moderator analyses showed that advanced age and comorbidities, including hypertension and stroke, were significantly associated with higher malnutrition prevalence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Approximately one in four older adults with sarcopenia experienced malnutrition, with the greatest burden observed in hospital settings. These findings underscore the need for routine nutritional screening in older adults with sarcopenia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Prevalence of malnutrition among older adults with sarcopenia: a meta-analysis and moderator analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Research has established that while most older adults use information and communication technologies (ICTs), loneliness and social isolation in later life is a pressing issue. Studies of older adults’ ICT use has largely been cross-sectional, focused on their attitudes and preferences, and conducted with white, well-educated individuals who were disproportionately aged 65 to 75. Using an intersectional life course perspective, the purpose of our study was to understand the meanings that diverse older adults attributed to ICTs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We purposively recruited and conducted in-depth, semi-structured qualitative interviews with 20 diverse men and women, aged 65 to 89. They were asked about experiences of social connection, disconnection, and use of ICTs over time. Interview transcriptions were coded and analyzed using interpretative description.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants shared stories underscored by wonder and fascination related to the arrival of ICTs into their homes and workplaces over the life course. In later life, they suggested that ICTs were important for connection and alleviating loneliness and social isolation as they allowed for instant, direct, and affordable communication. However, they also regarded ICTs as a source of disconnection as they undermined intimacy, spontaneity, and full social participation, especially for those with disabilities or limited finances.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings illuminate the importance of examining diverse older adults’ perceptions and experiences in a life course perspective. They also point to the need for training opportunities, improved technology design, and recognition from policy makers and service providers of older adults’ social connection preferences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Social connection and disconnection: Older adults’ life course perspectives on information and communication technologies

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In health care settings, immigrant older adults who are not fluent in English may not be able to fully express their problems, even with a translator, because there are important phrases about health problems in their native language that do not directly translate to concepts in English. This issue is particularly important for immigrant older adults, especially recent immigrants, who might experience limited English proficiency and rely heavily on health care services. For example, Chinese expressions, such as “心累” and “气堵,” and Spanish idioms, such as “sentirse agüitado” and “achicopalado,” roughly translate to different types of emotional distress but do not have accurate English translations. These linguistic barriers affect both psychological and physical health outcomes. This paper briefly describes different types of culturally-embedded metaphors, idioms, and linguistic framing commonly used by immigrant older adults in the US, especially those who speak Mandarin and Spanish. We then highlight that even with a good translator, these phrases lead to barriers in effective healthcare services. As a result of these translational issues, immigrant older adults may experience misdiagnoses and improper treatments, thereby decreasing patients’ willingness to seek help. We highlight the need for more research on this issue of culturally based descriptions of health issues, particularly psychological distress. While prior research documents these barriers, it does not provide direct causal evidence of how these concepts influence diagnosis and treatment outcomes. Doing so would provide a better understanding of how linguistic factors affect mental and physical health, guiding more inclusive, culturally sensitive solutions.</jats:p>
title: Psychological and health consequences of difficult-to-translate concepts among immigrant older adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>African Americans (AAs) are twice as likely as White Americans to develop Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) but half as likely to receive a timely diagnosis. Factors contributing to underdiagnosis among AAs include lack of healthcare access and provider bias, but little is known about attitudes, beliefs, and perceptions that may be patient-related drivers of dementia underdiagnosis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We performed a scoping review of attitudes, beliefs, and perceptions regarding ADRD among AAs by searching PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, and Black Studies Periodicals Database from 2002 to 2024. Eligible studies were written in English and discussed attitudes, beliefs, or perceptions toward ADRD among AAs in the United States. A primary reviewer identified key themes, which were then discussed and summarized by the team.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Forty-nine studies met inclusion/exclusion criteria after title, abstract, and full manuscript review. We identified six themes: AAs display gaps in knowledge about dementia; inclusive resources and support can help address the knowledge gap; stigma and losing autonomy are important barriers to seeking care; uncertainty in the relationship between the AAs and medical communities is an additional barrier; the AAs community has strengths that can be leveraged to support earlier dementia diagnosis if used carefully; and the AAs community is not monolithic.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>It may be possible to address dementia-related disparities in diagnosis by leveraging underlying barriers and facilitators within the AA community. Additional research is needed to understand variations in attitudes, beliefs, and perceptions toward ADRD among AAs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Amplifying the voice of a community: a scoping review of attitudes, beliefs, and perceptions among Black and African Americans about dementia

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined racial/ethnic and language-based differences in the Adult Protective Services (APS) process using the standardized Identification, Services, and Outcomes (ISO) Matrix tool to measure maltreatment identification during investigation, services, and outcomes post-intervention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data from two California county APS programs for adults aged 65 and older (n = 1,330) were analyzed. Measures included maltreatment allegations (self-neglect, neglect by others, financial abuse, emotional abuse, physical abuse), pre-test ISO Matrix scores, substantiation decisions, service types, and change in ISO Matrix scores from pre-test to case closure. Logistic regression models produced odds ratios (OR) by language (reference: English) and race/ethnicity (reference: White), adjusted for multiple comparisons.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>After adjustments, only financial abuse allegations were significantly higher among Black/African American clients than White clients. Emotional abuse pre-test scores were lower for Asian (OR: 0.45), Hispanic (OR: 0.39), and higher for non-English-speaking (OR: 2.18) clients, while self-neglect scores were lower among non-English speakers (OR: 0.57). There were no differences in substantiation decisions, service types, or ISO Matrix change scores across language or racial/ethnic groups. Change scores were influenced by client engagement and initial severity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study, one of the first to use a standardized tool to assess APS disparities, found equitable substantiation and service provision across race and language groups. Financial abuse allegations were more frequently reported among Black/African American clients, consistent with previous research. Emotional abuse varied by race and language, suggesting avenues for future research on cultural factors in abuse perception.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Using a standardized tool (ISO-Matrix) to assess differences in the Adult Protective Services process by client race/ethnicity and English language acquisition

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study identified latent domains and usage-breadth patterns of everyday digital technology (EDT) engagement among older adults and examined their concurrent and prospective associations with cognition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analytic sample comprised 2,910 adults aged ≥65 who completed the 2020 Leave-Behind Questionnaire of the Health and Retirement Study. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses identified latent domains across 31 digital activities, and latent class analysis (LCA) identified subgroups differing in engagement breadth. Structural equation models and class-based models examined associations with concurrent (2020) and prospective (2022) cognition, adjusting for prior cognition (2018) and other covariates.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four domains—information access, routine tools, social engagement, and logistic tasks—were identified and confirmed. The domains were intercorrelated and loaded on a second-order general factor, reflecting a graded propensity toward digital engagement. LCA distinguished low-, moderate-, and broad-use groups, with engagement broadening in a patterned way in which the more demanding logistic tasks were endorsed least often, even among moderately engaged users. The general EDT factor, selected domain factors, engagement breadth, and digital gaming were positively associated with concurrent cognition, but none prospectively predicted cognition after adjustment for prior cognition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>EDT engagement is best understood as a graded propensity that varies primarily in breadth. Its concurrent associations, absent prospective prediction over a two-year interval, are more consistent with cognitive status shaping EDT engagement than with short-term cognitive benefits of EDT engagement. These findings caution against strong claims that digital engagement preserves cognition, while supporting older adults’ digital participation may remain valuable on other grounds.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Beyond Digital Access: Domains and Breadths of Everyday Digital Technology Engagement and Associations with Cognition Among Older Adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The rapid global expansion of digital technologies has reshaped everyday life across generations, yet the role of smartphones in older immigrants’ social well-being remains insufficiently understood. Drawing on the sociotechnical perspective that ageing and technology are co-constituted, our study examines how Mandarin-speaking older immigrants in Canada use smartphones to overcome social isolation and sustain social participation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were obtained from 102 qualitative interviews conducted across seven Canadian cities as part of the Inclusive Communities for Older Immigrants (ICOI) project. The data were analysed using a hybrid deductive–inductive thematic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three overarching themes were identified: experiences of social isolation, shaped by linguistic, cultural, and seasonal barriers; smartphones as tools for social connection; and smartphones as facilitators of social participation, enabling both online engagement and the coordination of in-person activities. Study findings demonstrate that smartphones operate not merely as communication devices but as sociotechnical infrastructures that sustain belonging, enable local and transnational connectivity, and support mutual aid among older immigrants. At the same time, they complement rather than replace in-person interaction, with many participants preferring face-to-face social engagement when feasible.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to critical gerontology and migration scholarship by illustrating how digital technologies address social isolation among older immigrants and highlights the need for culturally and linguistically tailored digital inclusion initiatives that promote equitable ageing in diverse societies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Smartphone Technology, Social Network Maintenance and Social Participation among Mandarin-speaking older immigrants in Canada

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Population aging, delayed marriage, one-person households, and weakening assumptions of spouse-based care make unpartnered aging an emerging concern in Taiwan. This study examined how unpartnered middle-aged adults in urban Taiwan prepare for later life and developed two grounded models of solitary aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A convergent, qualitatively weighted mixed-methods design was used. Eleven unpartnered adults aged 43–56 completed interviews and questionnaires assessing demographics, subjective aging, personality traits, social connectedness, isolation, loneliness, financial adequacy, health status, and preferred later-life care. Interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, with Selection, Optimization, and Compensation and person–environment fit used as sensitizing frameworks. Quantitative indicators were integrated through theme-by-measure comparison.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants were predominantly female, educated, never married, and childless. Findings were synthesized into two models. The Lifestyle Model of Solitary Aging conceptualizes solitary aging as organized around autonomy, growth, and life purpose, while shaped by psychosocial adaptation and structural conditions. The Technology-Enhanced Solitary Aging model specifies how smart-home systems, digital communication tools, and health-monitoring devices may support autonomy, safety, and emotional connection when usability, accessibility, and familiarity are present. Across both models, participants used education, financial planning, health maintenance, selective social engagement, and technology to preserve independence, yet these strategies were constrained by loneliness, care uncertainty, policy gaps, and usability barriers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The models extend Selection, Optimization, and Compensation to nonspousal aging contexts by showing that compensation is relational, technological, and infrastructural. Policy should link care navigation, housing, community belonging, and accessible technologies without presuming family support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Aging Alone: Lifestyle and Unmet Needs Among Unpartnered Middle-Aged Adults Preparing for Later Life in Urban Taiwan

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Driving retirement is an increasingly significant life transition for older adults, yet few plan for this change despite its emotional, practical, and social implications. Older adults commonly experience mobility challenges, diminished wellbeing, and strong negative emotions—including grief, frustration, and loss of identity—when they stop driving. The dual process model of coping with bereavement offers a useful framework for understanding this transition, as it distinguishes between loss-oriented stressors (emotional reactions to giving up driving) and restoration-oriented stressors (adapting to new daily routines). This study examined the applicability of this model within a workshop-based intervention designed to support older adults in planning for and coping with driving retirement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty-five participants completed an evaluation of an evidence-informed, three-hour workshop addressing emotional, practical, and mobility-related aspects of the transition, through surveys before, one week after, and six weeks after the intervention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Content analysis of free-text responses revealed that participants’ experiences aligned strongly with the dual process model. Immediately after the workshop, participants reported reduced grief and practical concerns, increased consideration of alternative transport options, and greater validation of their emotional responses. Over time, many participants began trialling new mobility strategies and demonstrated shifts in perspective, indicating movement toward restoration-oriented coping.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings suggest that structured, psychologically informed interventions can support healthier adjustment to driving retirement. Such programs should address both emotional and practical components of the transition and be offered early to allow adequate time for planning and adaptation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Thriving Without Driving: Exploring the Impact of a Driving Retirement Intervention on Older Adults Through a Dual Process Model of Coping with Bereavement

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In England and Wales, coroners issue Reports to Prevent Future Deaths (PFDs) when an inquest identifies concerns that future deaths may occur unless action is taken. Although PFDs have increasingly been used to study preventable deaths in other contexts, care home deaths have remained largely unexamined. This study examined coroners’ construction of neglect in care home deaths involving older adults and considered the implications for future prevention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We undertook a Foucauldian Critical Discourse Analysis of 15 publicly available PFDs published on the Courts and Tribunals Judiciary website between 2018 and 2022. The reports concerned deaths of adults aged 60 years and over in which neglect formed part of the inquest conclusion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Coroners constructed neglect in two principal ways. “Dark room” neglect referred to immediate danger associated with residents being left unobserved or exposed to acute hazards. “Forgotten space” neglect referred to cumulative omissions, missed opportunities, and prolonged deterioration. Both constructs were aligned with a discourse of risk prevention that privileged institutional oversight, assessment and management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings reveal tensions between dominant and alternative discourses regarding risk and neglect in care homes. PFDs made some risks highly visible while rendering others less visible, particularly the relational and organisational conditions in which neglect develops. Greater attention to family knowledge, frontline staff experience, and cumulative deterioration may support collaborative approaches to prevention in care homes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: A discursive analysis of coroners’ construction of neglect in care home deaths

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to design and conduct an exploratory evaluation of an evidence-informed workshop series to promote the holistic well-being of late middle-aged and older adults with diverse sexual orientations, gender identities, gender expressions, and sex characteristics (SOGIESC) in Thailand.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The intervention, informed by the Minority Stress Model, the Transformative Learning Group Facilitation Model, and Experiential Learning Theory, focused on reducing loneliness and enhancing psychological, physical, social, and spiritual well-being by creating affirming, psychologically safe spaces. A non-randomized, single-group pre–post mixed-methods design was employed with 28 diverse SOGIESC participants aged 51–74. Quantitative data were collected using validated loneliness and well-being measures, while qualitative data from in-depth interviews were analyzed thematically.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants showed significant within-group reductions in emotional and social loneliness, with median scores decreasing by 1.0 point on a 3-point scale and large effect sizes (rrb = −.684 and −.725, respectively). Significant improvements were also observed in psychological, physical, and spiritual well-being, with moderate-to-large effect sizes (rrb = .460, .673, and .406, respectively). Qualitative findings highlighted the transformative role of social support, belonging, and affirmative community spaces in fostering self-acceptance and collective empowerment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These exploratory findings suggest that friendly space workshop interventions show promise in addressing loneliness and enhancing multiple dimensions of well-being among older adults with diverse SOGIESC. The findings also highlight the need for ageing and social policies that move beyond individual self-care toward relational, community-based, and structurally supportive models of well-being and inclusion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Reducing loneliness and enhancing well-being among gender and sexually diverse late middle-aged and older adults: An evidence-informed group intervention

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mobility limitations in later life can disrupt social engagement and increase loneliness, but trajectories may differ depending on whether limitations remain or individuals recover. This study examines loneliness trajectories around the onset of mobility limitations, focusing on differences by limitation duration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe were used to analyse 4,109 adults aged 65+ who experienced the onset of mobility limitations, of whom 2,018 recovered within two years. A reference group of 8,197 individuals had no mobility limitations. Loneliness was measured up to two years before and four years after the onset. Linear spline mixed-effects models estimated trajectories by onset and limitation duration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Loneliness increased following the onset of mobility limitations. Individuals with persistent limitations showed continued increases, while those who recovered stabilised, though not returning to pre-onset levels.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that early interventions to mitigate mobility limitations may help reduce the risk of subsequent loneliness. Physical recovery does not restore social and emotional well-being. For those with persistent mobility limitations, targeted efforts to curb increasing loneliness trajectories could be especially beneficial.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Loneliness trajectories surrounding mobility loss: The role of disability duration

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Amenable mortality, deaths preventable through timely and effective healthcare, is a widely used indicator of health system performance, yet evidence is lacking on its individual-level determinants in Brazil.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used data from the Brazilian Longitudinal Study of Aging (ELSI-Brazil), a representative cohort of adults aged 50 and older. Deaths were classified as amenable using both the Brazilian and the Pan American Health Organization’s definitions. Semi-parametric competing risks regression modeled the hazard of amenable death while accounting for non-amenable death as a competing event and adjusting for covariates.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 872 deaths during follow-up, 30% to 39% were classified as amenable, with rates ranging from 2.5 (50–59 yrs) to 32.3 (80+) per 1,000 person-years. Older age, male sex, unpartnered status, lower income, multi-morbidity, and tobacco use were associated with higher risk of amenable mortality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Amenable mortality constitutes a substantial and inequitably distributed share of deaths among older Brazilians.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Amenable Mortality Among Older Brazilians: Evidence From the Brazilian Longitudinal Study of Aging (ELSI-Brazil)

                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To examine whether physical activity (PA) relates to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) both directly and indirectly through depressive symptoms and social isolation, and whether social isolation moderates this association.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This cross-sectional analysis used data from the 2011–2014 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 2,933; ≥60 years). Self-reported PA, depressive symptoms, and social isolation were assessed. MCI was defined as a composite cognitive score greater than one standard deviation below the sample mean.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Weighted path analysis showed that higher PA levels were inversely associated with MCI. Depressive symptoms and social isolation mediated this association. Social isolation moderated the PA–MCI relationship, with the inverse association being most pronounced among individuals with higher isolation levels.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PA is associated with MCI in older adults through psychosocial pathways, and social isolation shapes this relationship. Promoting PA may be particularly relevant for those experiencing social isolation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Psychosocial Pathways Between Physical Activity and Mild Cognitive Impairment in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: Mediation and Moderation Analyses

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare decision-making to improve clinical efficiency and patient risk assessment. However, emerging evidence suggests these tools may disadvantage older adults from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, potentially worsening health disparities. This scoping review examines how AI-driven healthcare decision tools affect health outcomes among socioeconomically disadvantaged older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Following the Arksey and O’Malley framework and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, I searched PubMed, CINAHL, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science for peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2025. Studies were screened using a Population, Concept, and Context (PCC) framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirty-three studies met inclusion criteria, revealing four themes: algorithmic bias in training data, socioeconomic and digital access barriers, differential outcomes by income and race, and governance gaps in AI deployment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Current AI healthcare tools risk reinforcing socioeconomic health disparities among older adults, highlighting the need for equitable design, policy oversight, and regulatory reforms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Algorithmic Inequity in Aging: How AI-Driven Healthcare Decision Tools Amplify Socioeconomic Disparities in Health Outcomes Among Older Adults

                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To identify the predictors of the technology-assisted behaviors older adults would consider implementing once encountered with a health concern and seeking help.                     <jats:p>Current uses of certain technological outlets were positively associated with the consideration of their use in the studied context, albeit to different extents.                   <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results suggest that technology familiarity, media richness, and communication culture that encourages/hinders media richness contribute to understanding of the considered emergency-related media behavior in later life.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The present study examined whether engagement in activities mediates the association between loneliness and memory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Participants (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">N</jats:italic>
                      >12,000; Age range: 34 to 93 years) were from three large longitudinal samples from the US and England. Measures of loneliness and demographic factors were obtained at baseline, cognitive, physical, and social activities were obtained from a second wave, and episodic memory was obtained from a third wave, 8 to 17 years later.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A meta-analysis indicated that loneliness was prospectively associated with worse memory performance at follow-up, and to less engagement in cognitive, physical and social activities. Less engagement in cognitive activities mediated part of the association between loneliness and worse memory performance and explained about 7% of this link. Physical and social activities did not mediate this association.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The present study provided replicable evidence that less engagement in cognitive activities is a pathway linking loneliness to worse memory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Loneliness and Memory: The Mediating Role of Cognitive, Physical, and Social Activities

                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Many older adults stop seeing a doctor despite having insurance and significant health needs. This study asks whether psychological distress predicts disengagement from care, beyond structural barriers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Using three waves of the Health and Retirement Study (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">N</jats:italic>
                      = 5,184 adults 65+), we model whether distress in one wave predicts no medical contact in the next, testing whether wealth weakens this link.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults with more psychological distress were significantly more likely to disengage from care, even accounting for demographics, resources, and health needs. This link was stronger among those with less wealth, suggesting money helps buffer the effects of psychological strain. The pattern held even when looking at change within the same person over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Psychological distress independently predicts disengagement from care, and this effect is stronger among financially disadvantaged older adults. Mental health screening in primary care could help reduce disengagement in this group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Why Do Older Adults Disengage From Routine Medical Care? Psychological Distress, Wealth Stratification, and Health System Disengagement in Later Life

                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To examine the association between living alone and receipt of routine checkups among older adults with disabilities in the United States and explore the role of social determinants of health (SDOH) in explaining this relationship.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Using 2023 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data, we analyzed adults aged 60+ with disabilities (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 56,619). Adjusted logistic regressions examined the association between living arrangement and annual routine checkups. Indirect effects of nine SDOH were tested.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults with disabilities living alone had significantly lower odds of an annual routine checkup compared to those cohabitating. The relationship between living alone and routine checkups showed significant indirect pathways through housing instability, transportation barriers, stress, and reduced social support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings underscore living alone as an important marker of routine checkup disparities and suggest that efforts to reduce disparities must consider the material and psychosocial conditions that structure how individuals engage with healthcare.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Living Alone and Routine Checkup Disparities Among Older Adults With Disabilities in the United States: The Mediating Role of Social Determinants of Health

                    <jats:p>With the median entry age of Retirement Living Communities (RLC) in Australia rising from 65 to 75 years, traditional models that excluded care services must pivot toward comprehensive service delivery spanning health and domestic support to facilitate ageing in place.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Residents identified growing appetite service provision for ageing in place including domestic assistance, meal preparation, technology support, and in-home care.                     <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults with diet-related chronic conditions often rely on family caregivers to implement dietary modifications in the home.                     <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted an online survey with 88 U.S. RDNs to evaluate RDNs’ likelihood of providing caregiver training, concerns about the training, and types of support they anticipate providing.                     <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RDNs (76.9%) were likely/very likely to provide caregiver training. RDNs anticipated providing general and condition-specific nutrition education and shopping/meal preparation skills training. Findings suggest potential for RDNs to implement structured caregiver training.</jats:p>

records.abstract: <jats:p>This scoping review examines literature on eHealth interventions for the dementia care triad, people with dementia, informal carers, and healthcare professionals that were developed or culturally adapted to address the needs of ethnic minority groups. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, searches were conducted in PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, Embase, and Google. Studies published before 2007 or in languages other than English or Dutch were excluded. Thematic analysis revealed an increase in publications since 2015, mainly from the United States, with mixed-methods studies focusing on videophone technologies. Most interventions were home-based and caregiver-oriented, with limited inclusion of people with dementia. Chinese American and Chinese Canadian groups were most frequently targeted. Reported outcomes emphasized feasibility and acceptability, alongside mental health aspects such as depression and caregiver burden. Gaps remain in geographical diversity, linguistic accessibility, and inclusion of people with dementia. Future research should prioritize culturally adapted, multilingual, and inclusive interventions to enhance equitable dementia care.</jats:p>
title: eHealth Interventions for Dementia in Ethnic Minority Groups: A Scoping Review

                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>

                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>One hundred full-text articles were reviewed, and 15 met eligibility criteria. The review revealed four types of formal services: care management programs, caregiver education/training programs, support groups, and respite services. Most services associated with reducing caregiver burden and behavioral problems focused on educating or training caregivers. Findings suggest that various formal services, especially when delivered in person, may help reduce caregiver burden and behavioral problems among care recipients. Evidence-based dyadic interventions are needed to support caregivers and their care recipients in community settings.</jats:p>

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS), including agitation, depression, anxiety, psychosis, apathy, and sleep disturbances, are highly prevalent in dementia and significantly contribute to carer burden, accelerated cognitive decline, and increased healthcare utilisation. Despite their clinical relevance, NPS often remain under-recognised and sub-optimally managed. This review synthesises current evidence on the prevalence of NPS in dementia, their functional and psychosocial impacts, and pharmacological and non-pharmacological management approaches.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library (2013–2025) identified observational and interventional studies, which were systematically reviewed and synthesised. Data were independently extracted and quality-assessed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Eighty-two studies (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 67,945) were included. Neuropsychiatric symptoms were highly prevalent, affecting approximately 78% of individuals with dementia. The most common symptoms were apathy (39%), agitation (35%), and depression (32%), with variation across dementia subtypes. Neuropsychiatric symptoms were associated with functional decline, increased risk of institutionalisation (aHR = 2.15), higher caregiver burden, and increased healthcare costs (approximately 38%). Multicomponent non-pharmacological interventions reduced symptom severity by 18–28%, while pharmacological treatments showed modest efficacy and were associated with increased adverse events. The certainty of evidence ranged from high (prevalence estimates) to moderate (psychosis and hallucinations) and low to moderate (pharmacological interventions).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Neuropsychiatric symptoms are highly prevalent in dementia and have a substantial impact on patients, carers, and healthcare systems. Individualised non-pharmacological interventions should be first-line, with pharmacological treatments reserved for severe or refractory cases. Early screening and intervention are essential.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Neuropsychiatric Symptoms in Dementia: Prevalence, Impact, and Implications for Care and Carers — A Systematic Review

                    <jats:p>To address gaps from limited disaggregated data and low research participation among Asian subgroups, we explored different recruitment approaches used in studies involving Asian American dementia caregivers by Asian subgroup and study methodology, and related challenges and strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scoping review followed the JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. We used seven databases and reference searching for studies targeting unpaid Asian American dementia caregivers, without restriction on publication year.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 78 articles representing 70 studies, most used qualitative or cross-sectional designs and targeted Korean and Chinese. Community organizations and centers were the most common recruitment channels. Challenges and strategies highlighted stigma and limited cultural sensitivity toward both dementia and research participation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Recruiting Asian American dementia caregivers is influenced by interconnected individual and structural factors rooted in cultural influences and inclusivity gaps in research. Researchers and clinicians should strengthen trust-based community engagement, community-verified registries, and culturally responsive infrastructure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Recruitment Strategies, Challenges, and Gaps in Reaching Asian American Dementia Caregivers: A Scoping Review

records.abstract: <jats:p>Drawing on conservation of resource (COR) theory, this study examines how workplace age discrimination affects older employees’ vitality at work and explores the mediating role of internal employability and the moderating role of subjective age. Using a three-wave time-lagged survey of 318 older employees in Chinese organizations, the results show that workplace age discrimination significantly undermines older employees’ vitality at work partially through internal employability. Moreover, subjective age moderates both the negative effect of age discrimination on internal employability and the indirect effect on vitality at work, suggesting that feeling younger serves as a protective psychological resource. These findings extend research on work vitality by identifying a detrimental contextual antecedent and highlight the importance of employability perceptions and subjective age in shaping older employees’ responses to age-related bias.</jats:p>
title: Workplace Age Discrimination and Older Employees’ Vitality at Work: Mediating Effect of Internal Employability and Moderating Effect of Subjective Age

records.abstract: <jats:p>Violence against older adults often occurs within domestic and family settings, but less is known about how these contexts vary by age and gender. This study examines the associations of age and gender with residential occurrence and family-related offending in Brazil. Using nationwide administrative health records for individuals aged 60 and older in 2024, we estimate logistic regression models for both outcomes. Women have higher odds than men of experiencing violence in residential settings and reporting family-related offenders. Older age is also associated with higher odds of residential occurrence across several forms of violence. By contrast, the age gradient in family-related offending does not extend across violence types and is concentrated mainly in psychological violence among individuals aged 80 and older. The findings show that the location of violence and the relationship between victim and offender follow different patterns across later life.</jats:p>
title: Trapped at Home: Individual and Situational Factors Associated With Violence Against Older Adults in Brazil

                    We examine whether material hardship has adverse consequences for older adults’ mattering, and further consider this association in the context of the quality and quantity of older adults’ social interactions. Random- and fixed-effects models estimated using structural equation modeling examine the association between material hardship and mattering in a nationally representative longitudinal survey (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">N</jats:italic>

records.abstract: <jats:p>The expected trajectory of parent-child relationships—parents investing in children for decades before eventually requiring their support—can take different shape when children’s adult independence is constrained. Integrating the intergenerational stake hypothesis with the concept of generational maturity, this study explored one such case: how mothers of adult children with disabilities and other conditions requiring extensive care experienced and/or anticipated the later stages of their parenting journey. A thematic frame approach organized analyses of interview data from 72 mothers of adult children (82% whose children had serious conditions, mean age = 57). Mothers expressed grave concerns about their future deaths, focusing on who would care for their children, and tried to cope with their anxiety and guilt by concretely planning for their deaths and their children’s futures. Some worried that their children might die first, including what their own lives would look like absent this closely identified maternal role.</jats:p>
title: Reflections on Death among Aging Mothers of Adult Children with Serious Conditions

records.abstract: <jats:p>Dental care utilization in later life may reflect changing health needs, access to healthcare, and social inequalities that persist across the aging process. We examined trajectories of dental care utilization before and after dementia diagnosis and evaluated whether these patterns differed by race/ethnicity and educational attainment. We linked Health and Retirement Study data with Medicare claims (1992–2020) among 2,838 dentate adults aged 65 years and older with incident dementia. Mixed-effects logistic regression models estimated changes in dental care utilization relative to the year of dementia diagnosis. Dental care utilization declined in the years preceding dementia diagnosis, increased immediately after diagnosis (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 1.45, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.04–2.03), and subsequently plateaued. Non-Hispanic Black participants had lower dental care utilization compared with White participants (AOR = 0.21, 95% CI: 0.10–0.44), although trajectories of change surrounding dementia diagnosis did not differ by race/ethnicity. Racial and ethnic disparities persisted even among participants with higher educational attainment. Dementia diagnosis represents a potential transition point associated with temporary increases in dental care engagement, but it does not eliminate longstanding disparities in oral healthcare utilization. These findings highlight the importance of examining oral healthcare access as part of broader aging-related inequalities and ensuring equitable integration of dental care into the continuum of care for older adults with dementia.</jats:p>
title: Structural Inequities in Dental Care Use Across Dementia Progression: The Roles of Race/Ethnicity and Education

records.abstract: <jats:p>Older LGBTQ+ drag performers remain largely understudied within gerontology and LGBTQ+ aging scholarship. This qualitative study explored how older LGBTQ+ drag performers make meaning of drag expression across the life course. In-depth interviews were conducted with 21 participants aged 50 to 90 residing in the United States. Analysis revealed seven themes related to drag identity, embodied aging, resilience, marginalization, generativity, and intergenerational relationships. Findings informed an emergent theory of drag as a lifelong identity process. Participants described drag not merely as performance, but as an evolving meaning-making system through which they negotiated identity. Narratives illuminated the coexistence of resilience and vulnerability as participants navigated ageism, dragism, HIV/AIDS survivorship, bodily change, and shifting community dynamics. Findings expand our understanding of LGBTQ+ aging by positioning drag as a relational, adaptive, and culturally situated life-course practice that sustains continuity of self while resisting marginalization and preserving queer cultural memory.</jats:p>
title: Sequins, Survival, and Selfhood: An Emergent Theory of Drag as a Lifelong Identity Process Among Older LGBTQ+ Drag Performers

records.abstract: <jats:p>Social adaptation is critical for healthy aging, yet few longitudinal studies examine multidimensional social adaptation trajectories and its’ predictors among Chinese older adults. Using four-wave panel data (2014–2020) of 1,990 older adults, we applied latent growth and group-based trajectory models to map social adaptation developmental patterns. Personal development adaptation exhibited a nonlinear declining trajectory, while ideological-cultural adaptation fell into four subgroups: gradual decline, stable low, initial decline with subsequent stabilization, and sustained moderate-to-high adaptation. Baseline education and self-rated health positively predicted initial personal development adaptation levels. Cognitive function showed consistent positive longitudinal effects on personal development adaptation and heterogeneous predictive links to ideological-cultural subgroup membership. Depressive symptoms negatively predicted personal development adaptation and only predicted membership in the sustained high-adaptation ideological-cultural subgroup. Friendship had no significant predictive effect on two dimensions. This study confirms domain-specific heterogeneity in older adults’ social adaptation and offers empirical evidence for targeted active aging interventions.</jats:p>
title: Multidimensional Trajectories of Social Adaptation Among Chinese Older Adults: Heterogeneous Pathways Shaped by Cognitive Function, Depression Symptoms, and Friendship

records.abstract: <jats:p>This qualitative study explores how older adults (aged 65 and above) experience and perceive ageism in their everyday lives. records.abstract: <jats:p>As China's middle-aged and older population increasingly engages in grandchild caregiving, this study examines its psychological implications through the lens of role theory, with particular attention to the mediating role of social participation. Based on three-wave panel data, the findings show that grandchild caregiving is associated with higher life satisfaction and lower levels of depressive symptoms and loneliness among older adults. Caregiving is also related to a broader range and higher frequency of social participation. Additionally, the mediating role of social participation is mainly observed for depressive symptoms and loneliness, whereas no significant mediation is found for life satisfaction. The results further indicate that these associations vary between urban and rural settings, with stronger direct associations among urban older adults. This study highlights the value of intergenerational caregiving as a means of mobilizing familial resources in elderhood and encourages policies that support older adults’ meaningful participation in family life, particularly in the realm of childcare.</jats:p>
title: Effect of Grandchild Caregiving and the Psychological Well-Being of Middle-Aged and Older Adults in China: The Mediation Effect of Social Participation

records.abstract: <jats:p>Using an observational longitudinal design, this study examined psychological well-being, activity satisfaction, and perceived social support among 91 middle-aged and older adults participating in community-based intergenerational activities in Taiwan. Across eight waves over 18 months, psychological well-being was assessed through mental health, subjective happiness, life satisfaction, and loneliness. Unconditional growth models showed no significant average linear change in any outcome, suggesting relative stability at the sample level. However, random-effect estimates indicated meaningful individual differences in initial status and, for some outcomes, rates of change. Activity satisfaction was associated with several well-being indicators, but its explanatory role for change was limited. Perceived social support, disaggregated into within-person fluctuations and between-person mean differences, was consistently associated with better mental health, higher happiness and life satisfaction, and lower loneliness. Findings position intergenerational participation as a relational context in which perceived support may be central to maintaining psychosocial well-being.</jats:p>
title: Psychological Well-Being, Activity Satisfaction, and Perceived Social Support Among Middle-Aged and Older Adults in Intergenerational Participation: An 18-Month Longitudinal Study

records.abstract: <jats:p>Successful aging involves not only health maintenance but also continued social functioning and adaptation. Global demographic aging requires a better understanding of the psychosocial pathways through which older adults achieve successful adaptation, especially within culturally specific contexts. Positive aging attitudes are consistently associated with enhanced adaptation outcomes across diverse populations, yet the pathways through which these cognitive-emotional orientations relate to behavioral adaptation remain underexplored. This cross-sectional study used latent-variable structural equation modeling (SEM) to test a sequential mediation model among 1,016 Chinese older adults across six provinces. Validated instruments assessed aging attitudes, social support, life satisfaction, and social adaptation. Bootstrap mediation analysis with bias-corrected confidence intervals (5,000 resamples) was conducted. Results showed that positive aging attitudes were positively associated with social adaptation both directly and indirectly through social support and life satisfaction. Social support served as the primary mediator (33.33% of the total association), followed by life satisfaction (14.03%) and a sequential pathway through both mediators (10.53%). The stronger mediating role of social support relative to life satisfaction is consistent with the emphasis on relational interdependence in Chinese collectivistic culture. These findings suggest that interventions aimed at improving social adaptation among Chinese older adults may benefit from jointly targeting aging attitudes, social support networks, and subjective well-being in a sequenced manner. The results support the value of integrating socioemotional selectivity theory and the convoy model in research on aging in China, while highlighting social support as a particularly salient correlate of adaptation in later life.</jats:p>
title: Positive Aging Attitudes and Social Adaptation Among Chinese Older Adults: Sequential Roles of Social Support and Life Satisfaction

records.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines how older adults experience and respond to climate change through a qualitative phenomenological approach in Eskişehir, Türkiye. In-depth interviews were conducted with 24 individuals aged 65 and above living in urban and rural areas. Participants perceived climate change mainly through rising temperatures, drought, and irregular seasonal patterns. Rural participants emphasized agricultural and water-related problems, whereas urban participants highlighted increasing heat, energy costs, and social isolation. The findings show that older adults develop adaptation strategies such as household adjustments and resource-saving practices, although their adaptive capacity is shaped by socioeconomic and health-related factors. By comparing urban and rural experiences, the study contributes to the climate gerontology literature by demonstrating how climate vulnerability is shaped by place-based conditions. Although limited to a small and context-specific sample, the study highlights the need for locally grounded and age-sensitive climate adaptation policies.</jats:p>
title: "The Seasons Changed, and So Did We": Older Adults’ Adaptation Experiences to Climate Change in Urban and Rural Contexts in Eskişehir, Türkiye

<jats:p>
                    Ageism is of increasing concern as the population of older adults increases globally. As such, understanding the influence of intergenerational contact between younger adults and older adults is crucial in reducing ageism. The current study explored intergenerational contact between young adults and older adults and perspective-taking as predictors for young adults’ ageist beliefs, utilizing Allport’s (1954) contact hypothesis as the theoretical foundation. Participants aged 18–26 (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">M</jats:italic>
                     = 23.07,
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">SD</jats:italic>
                     = 2.15) were recruited using Prolific Academic and responded to a quantitative survey including scales related to ageism, intergenerational/intergroup contact, perspective taking, and social desirability via Qualtrics. Results indicated that younger adult's contact with older adults predicted ageist beliefs, with the relationship mediated by the younger adult's ability to take the perspective of the older adult. Findings have implications for revising intergenerational interventions and future research. Furthermore, the study expands the contact hypothesis into the field of aging and ageism and calls attention to the role of perspective-taking in changing younger adult's ageism beliefs.
                  </jats:p>
title: Intergenerational Contact and Ageist Beliefs: Perspective-Taking as a Mediator

records.abstract: <jats:p>Financial planning (FP) is one of the leading challenges for retirees. Research shows a gap in how informal financial counselling (IFC), psychological empowerment, and risk aversion contribute to retirees’ FP in the post-retirement phase. This study aimed to examine the role of IFC in retirees’ FP, with psychological empowerment as mediator and risk aversion as moderator. A cross-sectional survey design was followed. Data were collected from 490 (66% male, 34% female) government retirees from Punjab, Pakistan. The analysis revealed that IFC significantly contributes to retirees’ FP. Additionally, psychological empowerment mediates the relationship between IFC and FP, highlighting the importance of empowering retirees to make financial decisions. Although risk aversion positively influences FP, it does not significantly moderate the IFC–FP relationship. The findings highlight the need for targeted interventions, such as workshops, seminars, peer-group discussions, and accessible financial counselling programs, to enhance retirees’ financial preparedness.</jats:p>
title: Aging and Financial Literacy: The Interplay of Informal Counselling, Risk Aversion, and Empowerment

records.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Background:</jats:bold>
                    Primary Progressive Aphasia (PPA) is a rare condition characterised by a gradual loss of language due to neurodegenerative processes including frontotemporal lobar degeneration and Alzheimer’s disease. Speech and language therapy is one of the main treatment options for people with PPA (PwPPA). International survey studies among speech and language therapists (SLTs) have revealed considerable shortcomings in treatment options for this patient group. To date, there has been no survey on speech and language therapy for PwPPA in Germany.
                    <jats:bold>Methods:</jats:bold>
                    We translated a survey that was originally developed to describe speech and language therapy for PPA in the UK into German and adapted it to the German healthcare system. The final 32-item survey covering demographics of SLTs and PwPPA, referral patterns, as well as diagnostic and therapeutic procedures, was distributed online.
                    <jats:bold>Results:</jats:bold>
                    Data from 46 SLTs, from 10 of Germany’s 16 federal states with experience in treating PwPPA were included. These 46 SLTs had treated 158 PwPPA in the last 24 months and reported working with PwPPA for >20 sessions on average. PwPPA were most frequently referred to speech and language therapy 2-3 years after symptom onset with word finding difficulties. Qualitative content analysis revealed barriers on multiple levels to access speech and language therapy. Informal assessments, including analysis of spontaneous speech, interviews with PwPPA and/or carers and screening of language and communication skills were reported as most frequently used. SLTs rated life story work, activity and participation-focused therapy and symptom-focused therapy. for language disorders as the most commonly used for PwPPA.
                    <jats:bold>Discussion:</jats:bold>
                    This study provides an overview of the current state of speech and language therapy for PwPPA in Germany. It shows that there is currently no clear pathway for PPA care that covers all levels of the
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">International Classification of Functioning Disability and Health</jats:italic>
                    and encompasses both assessment and treatment approaches. A comparison of the results obtained from this survey study with those from other similar studies in the UK, Turkey and Italy revealed both similarities and differences. Our findings underscore the need for further research, the development of standardized, evidence-based assessment and intervention tools, and targeted professional training.
                  </jats:p>
title: Mapping PPA Care: Results of a Survey Study on Speech and Language Therapy for People With Primary Progressive Aphasia Across Germany

records.abstract: <jats:p>Sexuality plays an important role for couples confronted with dementia and may support them to cope with the disease, to sustain the couple relationship and sustain a better experience of the caregiving situation. Nevertheless, the majority of spouse caregivers report a decline in their sexual satisfaction. The objective of this study was to investigate the personal, interpersonal, social, and cultural factors related to sexual dissatisfaction (SD) in spouse caregivers of persons with dementia, as well as the relationships between these factors. This online study included 64 participants who completed questionnaires assessing these variables. A multivariate path analysis approach was used to examine the complex associations between factors. Results showed that conjugal satisfaction was the only factor directly associated with SD. Two indirect pathways through conjugal satisfaction were identified: first, between positive dyadic coping and SD; secondly, between intra-individual vulnerability and SD. Social support was directly associated with intra-individual vulnerability and resources. The severity of the persons with dementia’s symptoms was related to intra-individual vulnerability. Age was not associated with SD. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of clinicians making an assessment of conjugal satisfaction and facilitating improvements in the quality of spousal interactions and degree of agreement, in order to increase the sexual satisfaction of spouse caregivers. Conjugal satisfaction may indirectly be reinforced through promoting more supportive dyadic coping and decreasing emotional vulnerability.</jats:p>
title: Identifying the Factors Associated with Sexual Dissatisfaction in Spouse Caregivers of Persons with Dementia: The Importance of Conjugal Satisfaction

records.abstract: <jats:p>This study explores a new clustered social housing concept for older people through the lens of social citizenship for people living with dementia. For people living with dementia citizenship occurs most evidently in the ordinary domestic and community spheres. Based on ethnographic fieldwork, including observations and interviews, our analysis reveals how the design of this concept supports creating care-collectives outside of the often prevalent medical view. A structural interprofessional meeting acts as an institutionalized coordination body which pro-actively monitors, coordinates and shapes collectives for residents to receive care and support and remain engaged with the community. Initiating care-collectives from signals (early changes in residents’ functioning and wellbeing) has potential for enacting citizenship for people living with dementia, by situating them in a broader effort to engage with, and be part of a community. However, in the cross-domain collaboration new dilemmas and ethical considerations arise around boundaries of professionals responsibilities, information sharing, and their amount of agency to tailor services for residents.</jats:p>
title: Organizing Social Citizenship for People Living With Dementia: A Community Case Study

records.abstract: <jats:p>This study explores how a tactile and play-based intervention, the Colorful Counting Brickers, fostered emotional and social engagement among older adults with dementia in a Taiwanese long-term care setting informed by relationally grounded care practices. Grounded in person-centered care and theories of embodied selfhood, the research employed a four-phase design process including rapid ethnographic immersion, iterative design development, expert consultation, and in-situ implementation. Thematic analysis of observations, caregiver interviews, and written reflections revealed that engagement was not a fixed behavioral response, but an emergent and relational process shaped by sensory interaction, peer reciprocity, and caregiver facilitation. Three key dimensions emerged. First, embodiment was evident as residents engaged through tactile exploration, affective responses, and gestural interaction. Second, relationality enabled peer reciprocity, including imitation, turn-taking, and spontaneous assistance. Third, immediacy was apparent as caregivers adjusted facilitation strategies in real time through emotional attunement and embodied familiarity. The study introduces the concept of co-design-in-practice to describe these situated and informal design contributions enacted by caregiving staff. This research contributes to the field of dementia care by reframing caregiving as a form of design agency and by emphasizing the relational and culturally embedded nature of engagement. It advocates for a shift from designing isolated products to designing with and through everyday care practices. This perspective informs a more inclusive and practice-sensitive model of participatory dementia innovation that recognizes the experiential expertise of caregivers and the lived realities of those they support.</jats:p>
title: Designing Engagement in Dementia Care: Embodied Participation, Situated Adaptation, and Co-Design-In-Practice

records.abstract: <jats:p>Volunteering has been proposed as a way for people with young onset dementia to engage in personally meaningful activities; promoting social connections and creating opportunities to actively participate in the community. However, people with young onset dementia are typically positioned as dependent on volunteers, rather than being recognised as a resource. A social citizenship approach challenges this positioning; illuminating the contribution that people with young onset dementia can make when appropriate support is available. However, there is little understanding of how to facilitate volunteering for people with young onset dementia. This study was co-produced by The Smarties, a team of six researchers living with young onset dementia and two facilitators. Together we explored how people with young onset dementia volunteer in the UK, the benefits and barriers, and how access to volunteering can be improved. Audio data of people with young onset dementia discussing their experiences of volunteering were used from the Dementia Diaries project. The data were co-analysed with the co-researchers living with dementia. Three themes were developed that highlight the importance of valuing the volunteer; encompassing what they bring to the volunteering from their past, what they gain from it in their present, and for what they could achieve in the future. This research contributes to the limited pool of literature demonstrating how volunteering could be a way for people living with young onset dementia to engage in personally meaningful activity. It highlights how volunteering can be a practice of social citizenship, empowering people with dementia to take control of their narrative by learning new skills, building solidarity with peers, and celebrating unique interests and identities. We share practical recommendations guided by the understanding that for volunteering to be accessible to people with young onset dementia, then ensuring disabling structures and practices are recognised and removed is paramount.</jats:p>
title: Volunteering as Meaningful Activity for People Living With Young Onset Dementia: A Thematic Co-Analysis
